layered-architecture.title: Welcome to The layered architecture of networks, part of Computer Networks & Architecture.
layered-architecture.idea: Interviewers ask about layers because misuse of the model is the root cause of a large share of real network bugs: a VPN that breaks at one layer, a firewall rule that assumes a port means a service, a TLS inspection appliance that changes certificates. The model is how engineers argue about which layer a problem belongs to — and therefore whose job it is.
layered-architecture.example: Requesting a page from a server produces a stack of headers. Reading the capture from the outside in shows exactly what each layer decided. The Ethernet frame carries the MAC addresses of your machine and the gateway — not of the server, which is thousands of kilometres away. Inside it, the IP header carries your address and the server's, and that pair stays constant end to end. Inside that, the TCP header carries ephemeral source port 51932 and destination 443, and a sequence number. Inside that, TLS carries an encrypted record, and only at the far end is the HTTP request visible. Notice the pattern: link addresses are rewritten at every hop; IP addresses are not. That is the whole architecture in one sentence, and it is why a traceroute shows a chain of routers while the destination address never changes.
layered-architecture.challenge: Choose one widely used protocol — HTTP/2, QUIC, WireGuard or MQTT — and write a two-page architecture note describing which layers it touches, what it assumes about the layers below, which boundary it deliberately crosses, and what that gains. End with the failure modes that design creates, and how you would monitor for them.

routing-and-switching-internals.title: Welcome to Routing and switching internals, part of Computer Networks & Architecture.
routing-and-switching-internals.idea: This is the layer where design decisions are made and outages begin: a route advertised to the wrong neighbour, a VLAN that was never trunked, an MTU set below what the tunnel in the middle can carry. None of these are visible in a simple ping, which is exactly why engineers who understand forwarding debug in minutes and everyone else replaces hardware for a week.
routing-and-switching-internals.example: Read ip route/route print from the top down and remember that only the prefix length decides the winner. The first three lines are the local subnets, then a default route via the gateway. A host is unreachable when the table has no matching prefix at all — you will see the OS report "Network is unreachable" rather than a timeout, and that distinction is diagnostic gold: no route is a local table problem; timeout means a route existed and something beyond it dropped the packet silently. Now add the classic failure: a VPN pushes a route for 10.8.0.0/24, and suddenly a user cannot reach the internal payroll server at 10.8.0.17 that they reached before. Both routes match — the VPN's /24 and the office's /16 — and longest prefix match sends the traffic down the tunnel, where nothing answers. Reading the table with its prefix lengths makes the cause obvious in seconds; pinging in the dark never would.
routing-and-switching-internals.challenge: Design the addressing and routing plan for a three-site organisation: subnets per site and per function (staff, servers, guests, cameras), the routes each site's router needs, the metric or policy for choosing between two ISPs, and the MTU and MSS settings for the tunnel between sites. Write it as a configuration note another engineer could implement, including the two failure modes your plan tolerates and the one it does not.

subnetting-and-redundancy.title: Welcome to Subnetting, segmentation and redundancy, part of Computer Networks & Architecture.
subnetting-and-redundancy.idea: Subnetting looks like arithmetic homework until the moment you have one /24 left, eight departments, and cameras that must not share a broadcast domain with staff laptops. Then it is a design exercise with consequences: a badly planned subnet means renumbering a building later, or flattening the network and losing the ability to filter anything.
subnetting-and-redundancy.example: The requirement: 60 staff devices, 20 guest devices, 12 cameras, 8 printers, 2 servers, 4 wireless access points, one fibre uplink, and a facility network for the lab equipment. Start from a private block and allocate by size, largest first, leaving room to grow: give each floor's staff a /25 (126 hosts) — two floors, two subnets, so a broadcast storm on one floor does not affect the other. Cameras on a /28 (14). Guests on a /26, isolated from everything except the internet. Servers on a /27. The lab equipment on a /28. Uplinks and switch management on /30 or /29 slices, one per device. Then write the rule set that segmentation enables: guests → internet only; staff → servers and internet; cameras → nothing except the recorder and NTP; management ports → admin subnet only; all inter-subnet traffic through the layer-3 switch or firewall, where it can be logged. Finally, the resilience plan: a UPS sized for 20 minutes at the measured load, dual power supplies to the core switch, a 5G failover router, and a written, rehearsed instruction card for what staff do when the main link dies.
subnetting-and-redundancy.challenge: Produce a complete network design document for a two-floor organisation of your choice: a subnet plan with addresses and sizes, a device inventory with static and DHCP ranges, a segmentation policy expressed as rules, a redundancy plan justified against cost, and a measured capacity estimate for the uplink. Present it as if a client were paying for it, and be explicit about one trade-off you accepted rather than solved.

network-performance-and-observability.title: Welcome to Network performance, monitoring and failure, part of Computer Networks & Architecture.
network-performance-and-observability.idea: "The network is slow" is not an observation, it is a complaint. Turning it into a measurement — which hop, which direction, which time of day, which application, and what the numbers were before — is what network engineers are paid for. This lesson builds the toolkit: what to measure, how to interpret it, and what to watch continuously so that problems are known before users report them.
network-performance-and-observability.example: A user reports that the platform is slow. Four measurements, in order, take five minutes and produce a defensible answer. Start with latency and loss over a minute to the gateway, the ISP's first hop and the destination. mtr combines traceroute and ping and shows loss per hop and per hop cumulative — the key skill is reading column by column: loss that appears at hop 3 and continues to the end is a real problem at hop 3; loss that appears only in the last column is at the destination or beyond. Then measure capacity with iperf3, once against the gateway and once against an external reference. If the LAN gives 940 Mbps and the external path gives 12 Mbps on a 50 Mbps plan, the LAN is innocent and the wide area is the suspect. Then look at the browser's own numbers. A page that spends 1.8 s in "waiting for server response" is a server or database problem, not a network one; a page that spends its time in connection setup is latency; a page slowed by many parallel requests is a caching or bundling problem. Finally, check utilisation and flows on the uplink at the time the complaint happened. A backup job that runs at 14:00 and saturates the link is a scheduling problem, and the fix is a policy change, not new hardware.
network-performance-and-observability.challenge: Take one real "slow network" complaint and produce an evidence pack: a timeline of when it happens, latency and loss graphs from at least two vantage points, a throughput measurement on the LAN and the WAN, the top talkers at that time, and a written conclusion naming the cause and the fix with its cost. If your conclusion is "the ISP", show the measurement that proves it and would survive a support argument.
